title: Modules courbes elliptiques en caractéristiques ≠2 : notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
This page continues the previous one. There, a dihedral group D of order 8 (written 'D_4') was attached to its set S of four non-central involutions. Multiplying by the central element a is a fixed-point-free involution x ↦ x' on S, the 'antipodism', which makes S the vertex set of a combinatorial square Q_D. The functor D ↦ Q_D was asserted to be an equivalence of groupoids, with a presentation recovering D from (S, x ↦ x'). Grothendieck then begins a linear-algebra description of the 'structure of square' on S: an affine plane over F_2 (a torsor under a rank-2 F_2-space V) together with a nonzero linear form.

On this page:

(1) Lines over F_2. For V of rank 2 over F_2, a nonzero α ∈ V* is the same as a subset of V that is a basis, namely α^{-1}(1) = V \ Ker α. So a pair (V, α) is the same as a 2-element set C, with V ≅ F_2^C. Under this identification α is the sum of coordinates and Ker α is spanned by the diagonal element (1,1) of F_2^C. Equivalently, the pair is a rank-2 space with a distinguished line or nonzero vector; over F_2 in rank 2, nonzero vectors of V and of V* correspond.

(2) Squares as pairs (C, S). Hence a combinatorial square (the antipodal involution on S is translation by the diagonal vector) is equivalent to a pair (C, S): C a 2-element set and S a torsor under F_2^C.

(3) Torsors as covers. A torsor under F_2^C = ∏_{c∈C} F_2 is a family (A_c)_{c∈C} of F_2-torsors (2-element sets). That is the same as a degree-2 cover A → C, with A a 4-element set carrying a fixed-point-free involution whose quotient is C. Then S ≅ ∏_c A_c is the set of sections of A → C.

(4) Incidence. Each section is a 2-element subset of A, giving an embedding S ↪ 𝔓_2(A) and thus an incidence relation between S and A.

Geometrically: S = vertices (4), A = edges (4), C = the two pairs of opposite edges, and D = S/antipodism = the two diagonals. A vertex is exactly a choice of one edge from each opposite pair, i.e. a pair of adjacent edges. The next page states the dual statement, A ≅ ∏_{d∈D} S_d with S → D of degree 2. This is the self-duality of the square (vertices ↔ edges) inside its automorphism group D_8. It yields a 'formulaire' of the sets C, D, S, A attached to a square.

The purpose, within notes on moduli of elliptic curves in characteristic ≠ 2, is presumably to encode combinatorially the auxiliary 2-primary level structures. Candidates are the rank-2 F_2-space E[2] with a distinguished line or point, or structures with D_8-symmetry related to 4-torsion. Each would then be described as a functorial set-theoretic gadget (C, D, S, A), adapted to descent and stacks.
errors: No mathematical error. Phrasing is slightly loose: 'the donnée of a couple (V, α) ... revient à un ens. C à deux éléments, à l'élément diagonal de F_2^C' compresses two statements. α corresponds to a basis C, while Ker α corresponds to the diagonal vector of F_2^C. Both are correct.
The transcription's '(à savoir V* \ {α})' does not make sense as written. The intended basis is α^{-1}(1) = V \ Ker α, the two vectors on which α takes the value 1.

ideas.what: A nonzero linear form on a rank-2 F_2-space is the same as a basis (α^{-1}(1)), so (V, α) ≅ (F_2^C, sum) with C a 2-element set; Ker α is the diagonal.
ideas.modern_name: elementary linear algebra over F_2; GL_2(F_2) ≅ S_3 acting on the three nonzero vectors

ideas.what: A combinatorial square (4 vertices with antipodal involution) is equivalent to a pair (C, S), with C a 2-element set and S an F_2^C-torsor.
ideas.modern_name: torsor description of a square; the dihedral group D_8 as the wreath product C_2 ≀ C_2 = Aut of the structure

ideas.what: An F_2^C-torsor is a degree-2 cover A → C, with S = sections of A over C, embedding S ↪ 𝔓_2(A) (vertex–edge incidence); dually A = sections of S → D.
ideas.modern_name: Weil restriction / induced torsor along a finite étale map (here of finite sets); the vertex–edge duality of the square
ideas.usually_credited_to: folklore (the general formalism of torsors under induced groups is Grothendieck-school standard, SGA)
ideas.where_published: The general formalism of torsors and restriction of scalars appears in SGA 3/SGA 4-style texts; this specific combinatorial instance does not, to my knowledge.

deep.surprise_reason: Elementary, correct combinatorics of the square (vertices, edges, diagonals, opposite-edge pairs) phrased in torsor and cover language. It is typical Grothendieck style, as preparation for level-2 structures on elliptic curves, but contains nothing new or absent from the record.
transcription_corrections: Line 3: the parenthetical should read as the basis α^{-1}(1) (= V \ Ker α); '(à savoir V* \ {α})' is likely a misreading.

'Ainsi, la donnée d'une courbe ... (via l'un des revêtements)': in context, the object is very likely 'carré' (square), not 'courbe'. The parenthetical may be '(via l'un des sommets)' or similar; it is uncertain.
'et d'une dim 1/de V*' is likely 'et d'un élément ≠ 0 de V*' or 'd'une droite de V'; the meaning is a nonzero form or line.
The margin note says the two A_c (c ∈ C) play symmetric roles, relating the two descriptions via V and V*; it is largely illegible.
